newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan rebel demobilisation grinds to a halt.
newsitem.headline: Angolan rebel demobilisation grinds to a halt.

text.p: The demobilisation of thousands of former rebels in Angola has ground to a halt just a few weeks after it began, a U.N. official said on Thursday.
"De facto the process is on standby," an official of the U.N. Humanitarian Assistance Coordination Unit (UCAH) told Reuters. "Political conditions for demobilisation are not yet in place."

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, added that it was necessary to review the whole process of returning about 40,000 UNITA former rebels to civilian life while 26,300 others were integrated into a new unified national army.
UCAH, charged with coordinating demobilisation after two decades of civil war, has presented a report to the joint commission overseeing the 1994 peace accord which ended the fighting.
The demobilisation of child soldiers -- the first phase of a five-month process -- was originally scheduled to start in June, but only began three months later.
Now it had ground to a halt, the official said.
Around 7,000 soldiers under the age of 18 had gathered at U.N.- supervised assembly camps and of these just 494 had been demobilised.

The official said money was also running short because of the delays and up to $14 million was needed to cover expenses for relief organisations and to pay for water, food, health facilities and transport.
One of the problems was the failure of the Angolan government to pay cash promised to former fighters when they returned to civilian life, the official said.
Each was to be paid 30 percent of a $600 gratuity to help them start new lives, but the official said payment had stopped.

He also questioned UNITA's commitment to demobilisation, saying some child soldiers had reported intimidation by senior officers at the U.N. camps. Some of the young were discouraged from leaving or were persuaded to go to areas under UNITA control, rather than their homes.
More than 63,000 UNITA troops have registered and been disarmed at 15 U.N.-supervised camps, but U.N. figures show more than 13,000 of them have since deserted.
Half of them were under-age troops, the official said.
The U.N. Security Council has threatened to impose sanctions against UNITA after November 20 if it fails to meet obligations under the pact signed with the government two years ago.
UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi promised the U.N. in October that he would complete remaining steps in the pact within a month.
